lesson.title: When Two Nodes Become One: The Supernode Trick
lesson.summary: A floating voltage source between two non-reference nodes breaks the ordinary node voltage method, so a supernode wraps both nodes in one KCL boundary and adds the source's own voltage constraint.
lesson.body:
The node voltage method runs into a snag whenever a voltage source connects two nodes that are both away from the reference. A resistor lets you write its current directly from the two node voltages using Ohm's law, but a voltage source does not obey Ohm's law, so there is no resistance to divide by and no clean way to express the current through it in terms of node voltages alone. The fix is not to give up on KCL, it is to draw a boundary around both nodes at once, treating them as a single combined node called a supernode, and apply KCL to the whole boundary rather than to each node separately.

Two ideas make this work together. First, current is still conserved: whatever flows into the supernode from the rest of the circuit must flow back out, since charge cannot pile up inside the boundary, even though some of it is passing through the voltage source connecting the two nodes internally. Second, the voltage source itself gives you a free equation for nothing: since it directly fixes the difference between the two node voltages, you simply write that constraint, VA minus VB equals the source voltage, alongside the KCL equation for the boundary. Two unknowns, two equations, done.

Try this circuit: a 4 amp current source injects current into node 1. A 2 ohm resistor connects node 1 to ground, and a separate 2 ohm resistor connects node 2 to ground. A 6 volt source sits directly between node 1 and node 2, with the plus terminal at node 1. Node 1 and node 2 form the supernode. The KCL equation for the supernode boundary says the 4 amps entering must equal the current leaving through both resistors to ground: 4 equals V1 divided by 2, plus V2 divided by 2. The constraint from the source is V1 minus V2 equals 6, so V1 equals V2 plus 6.

Substituting, 4 equals (V2 plus 6) over 2, plus V2 over 2, which combines to (2V2 plus 6) over 2, or V2 plus 3. So V2 equals 1 volt, and V1 equals 7 volts. Check the source constraint: 7 minus 1 is 6, correct. Check the supernode KCL: V1 over 2 is 3.5 amps, V2 over 2 is 0.5 amps, and 3.5 plus 0.5 is exactly 4 amps, matching the source. As a bonus internal check, the current actually flowing through the voltage source branch itself must be 4 minus 3.5, or 0.5 amps, flowing from node 1 into node 2, and that is exactly the 0.5 amps node 2 needs to send to ground through its resistor. Every number is accounted for.

Supernodes are not an exception to the node voltage method, they are a required extension of it: any circuit with a floating voltage source, one not connected to the reference node, needs this trick, and most realistic multi source circuits have at least one. Mastering it is what makes nodal analysis, the general purpose procedure covered later in this chapter, actually general purpose. A helpful mental image is a soap bubble stretched around both nodes and the source that joins them: current can cross the bubble's surface freely through the resistor branches, but nothing can accumulate inside it, so whatever total current pierces the surface on the way in must pierce it again on the way out, regardless of how the current chooses to split internally between the two nodes.
